We analyze the discrepancies between objective measures (e.g., Green View Index (GVI)) and subjective scores (e.g., pairwise ratings), examining whether they can be explained by a variety of human and visual factors such as age group and spatial variation of greenery in the scene. The findings reveal that such discrepancies are comparable around the world and that demographics and personality do not play a significant role in perception. Further, while perceived and measured greenery correlate consistently across geographies (both where people and where imagery are from), where people live plays a significant role in explaining perceptual differences, with these two, as the top among seven, features that influences perceived greenery the most. This location influence suggests that cultural, environmental, and experiential factors substantially shape how individuals observe greenery in cities.

title: An integrated vulnerability-resilience framework for climate risk assessment in depopulating urban landscapes
abstract: • Coupled vulnerability and resilience shaped distinct neighborhood risk profiles. • Exposure is the primary driver of vulnerability in high-risk census tracts. • Strengthening disaster response capacity is most effective for high-risk areas. • A sensitivity analysis identifies actionable risk factors for targeted adaptation. • Impervious surface reduction is a key intervention for mitigating hazard exposure. Climate-related hazards are intensifying, exposing persistent limitations in prevailing risk assessment approaches that rely on static or exposure-centered formulations. The inadequate treatment of interactions between vulnerability and time-structured resilience capacities obscures policy-actionable mechanisms, limiting interpretability for local planning. These limitations are particularly pronounced in depopulating Midwestern Rust Belt cities, where long-term socioeconomic decline and infrastructure deterioration intersect with climate stressors in spatially heterogeneous patterns not resolved by static or aggregated risk measures. The goal of this study was to develop and apply an integrated climate risk assessment framework that distinguishes vulnerability and resilience as analytically distinct yet interdependent dimensions and examine their coupled dynamics in shaping neighborhood-scale risk profiles. Vulnerability and resilience were operationalized using spatially explicit indicators spanning five capital assets–social, economic, environmental, infrastructure, and health–to identify distinct vulnerability–resilience configurations. The framework was applied to census-tract-level data in Detroit and Cincinnati. The results reveal heterogeneous pathways of climate risk across urban contexts, demonstrating that neighborhoods with comparable exposure and sensitivity experienced different risk outcomes, depending on their phase-specific resilience capacities. Machine-learning analyses identified dominant policy-relevant drivers associated with higher-risk configurations, highlighting the influence of exposure conditions alongside the importance of disaster response and recovery processes in mitigating risk. Priority interventions include impervious surface reduction, wetland expansion, emergency services employment, and educational access. By modeling the coupled dynamics of vulnerability and resilience, this study advances a more interpretable and planning-oriented approach to climate risk assessment, supporting spatially targeted adaptation strategies in structurally disadvantaged urban environments.

title: Prioritising actions over space and time in multi-habitat ecological restoration: Insights from indicator species in coastal seascapes
abstract: Restoring multi-habitat landscapes requires decisions on habitat placement and sequence. Animal distributions can indicate landscape change, yet few studies have leveraged such data to inform landscape-scale restoration decisions. We investigated this using data describing fish assemblages from 13 estuaries and four coastal habitats (seagrass, mangroves, reefs, log snags) in southeast Queensland, Australia, over two years (n > 1000 surveys). Distribution models for five indicator species, fish abundance, fish richness, and harvestable fish abundance were combined to map habitat restoration benefits for all fish metrics in unison and constrained to suitable growth areas for each habitat for an exemplar estuary. Restoration, regardless of habitat type, had greater predicted benefits for fish when implemented at sites proximal to the ocean, and existing seagrass and mangroves. We then tested the effects of restoring the top 5% of sites, followed by the 5th to 10th percentile of sites for each habitat. For the top 5% prioritisation, rocky/oyster reefs should be restored first because they provide the greatest modelled benefit for fish (59.1% of the maximum theoretical outcome), followed by seagrass (43.8%), log snags (39.2%) and mangroves (35%). Updating the distribution models after restoring the top 5% of sites shifted the priority of habitats with mangroves becoming most beneficial and boosted outcomes by 20.6–30.8% compared to the original 5th to 10th percentile sites. Results underscore the importance of integrating remnant and newly restored habitat patches into restoration planning, emphasising that the strategic timing and placement of actions can maximise synergistic benefits.

title: Combating heat stress through urban planning: Integrated case studies for Lisbon and Islamabad
abstract: Open-access version of "Combating heat stress through urban planning: Integrated case studies for Lisbon and Islamabad", published in Landscape and Urban Planning. Abstract: Nature-based solutions are often proposed as adaptation techniques to heat stress and high temperatures in cities all over the world, but quantifications of their potential effectiveness are lacking. In Lisbon and Islamabad we co-designed, together with local stakeholders, a selection of urban planning strategies using commonly proposed green and blue infrastructure solutions from literature. Their effectiveness in reducing temperature and heat stress on climatological time scales were simulated using the UrbClim model, allowing spatial resolutions up to the meter-scale, while potential benefits for sleep loss, heat stress and heatwave exposure were quantified using CLIMADA. Green and blue infrastructure generally offer local relief with respect to heat stress, reducing heat stress days by up to 40%, mainly by providing shading from direct sunlight and by reducing land surface temperatures. Nighttime temperatures are most efficiently reduced by unsealing urban areas, while daytime temperatures benefit most from increases in high vegetation and trees (both up to 0.5°C). To maximize benefits for the population, urban planning strategies should focus on areas with highest population densities, as temperature reductions and heat stress relief quickly decay outside of the areas of intervention. Despite their proven positive effects, the investigated green and blue urban planning strategies clearly reveal limits to adaptation towards the future, especially in a Current Policies scenario, as they only offset part of the projected heat stress impacts.

title: Editorial Board
SECURE-NBS: A conceptual framework for integrated nature-based flood risk reduction
Planning for liveable cities across contexts: A comparative analysis of life satisfaction determinants in Hong Kong and Shenzhen
abstract: Creating liveable cities is a central ambition of contemporary urban planning, yet the determinants of urban life satisfaction (a widely recognised indicator of urban liveability) remain contested, particularly across different urban and regional contexts. This study examines the determinants of life satisfaction through a comparative lens, focusing on Hong Kong and Shenzhen, two neighbouring cities that represent distinct urban typologies within China’s Greater Bay Area. Drawing on survey data from 3,066 residents, we employ partial proportional odds and restricted cubic spline models to assess how built environment features, individual and household characteristics, subjective perceptions, and regional mobility each contribute to life satisfaction. The findings reveal both universal principles and context-specific mechanisms shaping life satisfaction. While factors such as greater living space and participation in cross-border leisure are positively associated with life satisfaction in both cities, effects of variables like gender, marital status, and homeownership are significant only in Shenzhen. Preferences for the built environment also diverge: Hong Kong residents place greater emphasis on urban form and access to green and blue spaces, whereas Shenzhen residents value functional diversity, transport accessibility, and lower development intensity. Analysis of non-linear relationships further shows that planning-related associations vary across intensity ranges, with distinct saturation points and trade-offs emerging in each city. Together, these findings highlight the importance of planning strategies that are sensitive to local context and attentive to both social and physical dimensions of urban life. The positive association between cross-border leisure and life satisfaction also underscores the growing relevance of regional connectivity for well-being in increasingly networked urban regions.

title: Association between urban ecological environment quality, socioeconomic disparity, and incidence of type 2 diabetes among middle-aged and elderly populations in the United Kingdom
Social media as a sensor: unraveling nonlinear drivers of perceived thermal comfort in Shanghai
Unequal access to cultural ecosystem services across urban greenspaces
PC-GAN: A deep learning framework for automated urban morphology design with spatial constraints to improve heat resilience
Unraveling threshold effects and hierarchical mechanisms of spatial mismatch between urban environment and subjective well-being in megacities
Greenery in the 15-minute city: Children’s walking accessibility and visual exposure to greenery in urban zones
abstract: • Integrating visual exposure to greenery (VEG) along walking routes into the 15-minute city framework. • 15-minute walking routes show lower VEG than routes exceeding 15 min. • Four categories of children’s walking environment based on walking accessibility and VEG. • VEG-based maps identify priority areas for preserving and replenishing greenery. Contact with nature has been weakly integrated into the 15-minute city concept, and children have largely been overlooked as pedestrians. A primary pathway for strengthening daily contact with nature may be visual exposure to greenery (VEG) along walking routes. The study jointly analyses children’s pedestrian accessibility to urban amenities and the greenness of their walking routes, and examines spatial variations in these combined characteristics across urban zones within a 15-minute city framework. We applied network and viewshed analyses to spatially explicit data on the residential locations of the entire population of children aged 7–15 (N = 48,266) living in Lodz, Poland. This enabled us to assess potential walking accessibility, defined as the shortest walking routes from children’s homes to eight types of urban amenities, as well as VEG along these routes in both close-up and distant views. We found a common tension between urban density and greenery: the more densely built-up an area, the more convenient the access to urban amenities, but the lower the VEG. However, the trade-off between greenery and densification is more nuanced. Post-socialist multifamily housing estates offer a promising balance, providing both walkable access to amenities and VEG for children. An integrated planning approach should move beyond proximity alone and allow for a more nuanced understanding of contact with greenery, explicitly accounting for seeing greenery during everyday walking trips. Context-sensitive planning is therefore necessary to capture the relationships between walking accessibility and VEG, and to better integrate proximity-based planning with urban greening strategies.

title: Non-linear responses of ecosystem service trade-offs to landscape heterogeneity: implications for spatially targeted landscape management in an urbanizing agricultural basin
Assessing the divergent impacts of urban shrinkage on carbon emissions: evidence from Chinese cities
Rethinking surrogate species for actionable biodiversity conservation: A scientometric review with a landscape planning-oriented pathway
The impact of person-environment fit from age-friendly neighbourhood on older adults' subjective wellbeing in China
abstract: The development of age-friendly neighbourhoods and the impact on wellbeing among older adults has attracted growing attention. However, the extent to which the congruence and incongruence between age-friendly neighbourhood attributes and older adults’ personal characteristics, represented by functional abilities, remains underexplored concerning subjective wellbeing (SWB). Based on survey and multi-source geographical data from 30 neighbourhoods in Guangzhou, China, this study examines the direct effects of nine domains of age-friendly neighbourhood environments on SWB using multilevel regression models. Drawing on person-environment fit (P-E fit) theory, it investigates how congruence between personal and environmental characteristics influences SWB. Using polynomial regression with response surface analysis, we test whether environments exert compensatory or enabling effects when person-environment congruence is lacking. Findings reveal that the green and blue environment, accessible environment, as well as communication and information domains are positively associated with higher SWB. Congruence between functional abilities and the provision of community support and health services is associated with higher SWB compared with incongruent situations. While greater congruence in the green and blue environment and in the communication and information domains is associated with higher SWB, a reverse U-shaped pattern is observed for the community support and health services domain, suggesting that greater healthcare resources combined with higher functional abilities are associated with lower SWB. Notably, compensatory effects predominately shape SWB in the green and blue environment and the communication and information domains. Overall, these findings identify key priorities for developing age-friendly neighbourhoods in urban China and underscore the need for domain-specific and ability-contingent frameworks applicable across diverse contexts.

title: Does urban compactness mitigate youth disconnection? evidence from U.S. Counties
The association between objective and perceived bird diversity and the mental health of minoritized communities living near disused parks in Detroit
abstract: • The role of biodiversity in the relationship between nature and human health remains unresolved, especially in underrepresented communities. • Potential associations between bird diversity and mental health, and the moderating effect of nature relatedness, were explored in Detroit, USA. • Objective and perceived bird diversity had a positive association with mental health. • Community-led greenspace restoration in Detroit that promotes diverse bird communities could improve mental health outcomes in minoritized neighbourhoods. Exposure to nature provides mental health benefits, yet the role of biodiversity is unresolved. The relationship between biodiversity and mental health has received some research attention but has yet to be explored thoroughly in minoritized communities where major health disparities occur. We explored the relationship between objective and perceived bird diversity and mental health in Detroit, USA. We collected mental health metrics, perceptions of neighbourhood bird diversity, systolic blood pressure, nature relatedness scores, and sociodemographic information from 209 adults across 11 Detroit neighbourhoods in 2023. To predict objective bird species diversity, we collected acoustic recordings from 10 random sites in each neighbourhood and identified bird vocalizations to species level. We found a negative association between anxiety and objective bird species richness (OR = 0.52, 95% CI [0.32, 0.83]) and between depression and perceived neighbourhood bird diversity (OR = 0.69, 95% CI [0.48, 0.99]). Nature relatedness was not a significant moderator of the relationship between bird diversity and mental health. Our results suggest that both perceived and objective bird diversity may promote positive mental health outcomes. These results signal an important role for greenspace rehabilitation in Detroit that promotes biodiversity and reduces barriers to nature for minoritized residents, thus enhancing social and environmental justice.

title: Urban plant communities shape plant–bird frugivory interaction networks through reduced connectance and increased modularity
Local and landscape effects on ant functional and taxonomic compositions across green spaces of a tropical metropolis
abstract: Urbanization is one of the main processes driving environmental transformation, altering the structure and functioning of biological communities across multiple spatial scales. In this study, we evaluated the effects of local and landscape variables on the taxonomic and functional composition of ants in different types of urban green spaces in the city of Salvador, Brazil. A total of 62 sampling points were surveyed across forest fragments, squares, streets medians, and vacant lots, using specific methods for both ground-dwelling and arboreal strata. We recorded 93 ant species distributed among 20 functional groups. Our results indicated that, at the local scale, leaf litter depth was the primary explanatory factor for both taxonomic and functional richness, as well as for functional composition. At the landscape scale, human population density and vegetation cover surrounding the sampling points influenced the distribution of species and functional groups, revealing contrasting patterns between specialist and generalist species. While arboreal, hypogeic, and fungivorous ants were more dependent on structurally complex and conserved habitats, epigeic, omnivorous, and some predatory species were favored in more simplified and heterogeneous environments. These findings highlight that biodiversity conservation in urban areas depends on integrated strategies across multiple scales, encompassing management practices that ensure local structural complexity alongside planning that promotes habitat heterogeneity at the landscape level. Overall, the study demonstrates that the arrangement and quality of urban green spaces play a central role in maintaining both taxonomic and functional diversity of ant communities in tropical cities.

title: Socio-economic and urban form characteristics driving urban agriculture development: A spatial analysis across 11 large European cities
abstract: Urban agriculture (UA) is a multifunctional land use that is thought to enhance urban resilience and sustainability while promoting community cohesion and connection to nature. However, its spatial emergence may have led to an inequitable distribution of these services due to largely unexplained factors driving its development. This study aims to uncover the conditions that might enable UA at a 1 km 2 scale in 11 large European cities. UA initiatives were mapped for each city based on a systematic manual web scrape. Negative binomial regression models were used to test the spatial relationship between UA count per km 2 and 14 socio-economic, land use, and urban form explanatory variables. The model was run separately for each city and then on the full dataset, uncovering differences within and between the cities. The intercity model suggests that UA is more likely found in greener, central neighbourhoods with lower property prices and lower proportions of locally born residents. The cities vary notably in their individual models, although the most common predictors also indicate that UA is found closer to the city centre and is often associated with urban green spaces (UGS). This may imply that coexistence of UA and UGS enhances and diversifies ecosystem services while protecting UA as a temporary land use. It also suggests that UA benefits community-seeking people living in the dense city centre without private gardens. However, there is not a consistent set of factors that imply UA presence, indicating other social and policy factors might be at play.

title: Assessing the potential to scale-up urban agriculture in the Global North
abstract: Urban agriculture (UA) is frequently promoted as a pathway to improve urban sustainability, food security, and resilience, yet cross-city evidence on its scalable, system-wide impacts remains limited and methodologically inconsistent. We assess the theoretical scaling potential and food–energy–water (FEW) metabolism implications of expanding low-tech UA across five Global North cities—London, New York City, Paris, Dortmund, and Gorzów Wielkopolski—using a harmonized two-part framework. First, we conduct 1-m resolution spatial multi-criteria suitability modeling, supplemented with sensitivity scenarios. Second, we upscale empirically derived site-level resource–yield “metabolisms” to quantify potential contributions to vegetable provisioning, resource demand, and nutrient cycling. Across base scenarios, 12–24% of city area is suitable for UA, with individual/home gardens comprising the dominant share of expandable space in every case. Under average observed yields, scaled UA could supply 16–95% of current non-tropical vegetable demand (and substantially more under high-productivity assumptions), while requiring relatively modest shares of city electricity use but potentially meaningful shares of potable water in smaller cities. Expanded UA could also absorb more than 100% of current vegetable food-waste streams via composting, indicating strong circularity leverage. However, participation requirements emerge as a primary constraint: labor availability and willingness limits feasible realization of these theoretical maxima. Together, results provide a transferable, cross-city methodology and identify policy-relevant leverage points—especially enabling home gardening, securing land tenure, supporting new farmers or gardeners, and pairing expansion with composting and water-harvesting practices—to design context-sensitive UA scaling strategies.

title: Deterministic processes result in clustered functional and phylogenetic river insect biodiversity along urbanization gradients in a (sub)tropical megacity
Editorial Board
Beyond one-size-fits-all: A spatiotemporal and user-stratified analysis of greenway influences on running activity
Densification in European city-regions: From observed patterns to actors and policy constellations
abstract: Urban densification is widely promoted as a strategy to limit land-take and provide housing, yet its sustainability and effectiveness remain debated. The impacts of densification depend heavily on the form of densification, but systematic knowledge about these forms and the policies and actors shaping them is still limited. To better understand this relationship, we present an approach to measure densification on the level of urban form through multi-temporal building data, which overcomes limitations for comparative research. We derive information on building change, housing form and project size which allows us to identify densification patterns. Through aggregation and visualisation, the observed patterns are discussed against the backdrop of actor constellations and institutions of land policy. To test the approach, we apply it to three city-regions in Germany, France and England. The interpretation of the spatial results reveals distinct patterns, which are found to be in line with knowledge on actors and policy across the regions, which we retrieve from existing literature on land policies in the context of densification. Predominantly large-sized development of detached housing in the Liverpool region are found, compared to large- to medium-sized apartment projects in Strasbourg and incremental densification in Dortmund. The analysis and interpretation of the study indicates for a viable inter-disciplinary approach to urban densification, as we uncover national characteristics in urban form and actors and policy, while relying on widely accessible data. Based on this, future endeavours for urban densification could develop policies targeted at specific actors and spatial patterns.

title: The green gap framework: Understanding non and low use of urban greenspaces
abstract: Despite the well-documented benefits of engaging with nature, up to a quarter of the UK population rarely utilises their urban greenspaces. This is despite evidence that those who engage the least with greenspace could derive the most significant health benefits from such interactions. Addressing this gap is a focus of the GroundsWell consortium, a large research programme that aims to transform access to urban green and blue spaces to improve health and reduce inequalities. As part of this initiative, this paper presents the development of a novel theoretical framework designed to identify and map the modifiable multilevel factors influencing non and low use. Employing an iterative process, the framework was developed through literature review, expert consultation, and stakeholder collaboration across practice, policy and research. It conceptualises barriers and facilitators across four interconnected domains: individual, social and community, physical environment, and political and societal. The framework illustrates how these domains interact to influence engagement, providing a tool for understanding the complex reasons behind non and low use of urban greenspace. Drawing on academic and non-academic sources, it demonstrates that urban greenspace planning, and design alone are insufficient if societal and social barriers persist. This framework has the potential to inform future policy, urban planning and management strategies, and research aimed at reducing inequalities in access to greenspace. It is designed as a dynamic tool that evolves in response to ongoing empirical research and practical applications, inviting further refinement by researchers, policymakers and practitioners to address health inequalities effectively.

title: Beautiful and rich – Visual attractiveness vs. Ecological approach of urban green areas
abstract: Contemporary management of urban green areas requires a comprehensive approach in many aspects. One of the key challenges is to design an aesthetic and attractive urban space while preserving maximum biodiversity. Hence, the objectives of this study were to (1) examine the relationships between visual attractiveness and species diversity, as well as (2) determine how plants’ biodiversity can be improved to be more attractive to the public. A landscape and species inventory were conducted for an urban park in Poznań, Poland. Based on this, the landscape was valorized, and biodiversity indices were calculated. Statistical methods were also applied to analyze relations, including PERMANOVA, the Kruskal-Wallis test, and PCA. The study confirmed that vegetation composition and vertical structure significantly influence biodiversity. Various levels of structure such as trees, shrubs, and low vegetation were important for both aspects studied. Landscape transformation affected both biodiversity levels and visual appeal, with pronounced effects in areas of low and high transformation. However, the high degree of management intensity in some areas promoted biodiversity and visual attractiveness. In the most visually attractive areas, numerous species with distinctive flower colors and leaf shapes forms were identified, potentially enhancing the subjective perception of the landscape. These findings are especially valuable for guiding the planning and design of urban green spaces, as they demonstrate how social expectations − such as aesthetic quality and recreational use, can be effectively integrated with environmental goals, particularly the conservation and enhancement of biodiversity.

title: A scoping review of participatory tools and practices in collaborative processes: Towards multi-actor collaboration in integrated landscape approaches
abstract: In this article, we ask how the different tools and practices used in participatory and collaborative processes could support multi-actor collaboration in integrated landscape approaches (ILAs). First, we conducted a scoping review to identify and synthesize literature on participatory and collaborative approaches related to forest, water, land and landscapes. Secondly, we analysed 130 articles to understand how and by which means these approaches engaged different actors in multi-actor collaborations. Our findings identified a wealth of different tools and practices available to support participatory and collaborative approaches, such as participatory mapping and modelling, games and visualizations, scenario development, and knowledge co-creation. Further, our scoping review identifies 30 articles about processes with core elements of collaborative governance, namely, principled engagement, shared motivation, and capacity of joint action. We argue that externally directed processes with short-term funding do not ensure multi-actor collaboration and a commitment towards ILAs. Both collaborative governance and ILAs demand administrative openness, cross-sectoral collaboration and recognize feedback loops to ensure evolving collaboration.

title: Urban metabolism as a pathway to advance Nature-based Solutions for climate-resilient cities
abstract: Rapid urbanisation has stimulated profound socio-economic transformation while intensifying systemic urban risks such as flooding and urban heat. These climate-induced stresses underscore the imperative of resilience-oriented urban frameworks. Existing research highlights Nature-based Solutions (NbS) as pivotal strategies for climate mitigation and adaptation, yet their widespread implementation remains constrained by persistent barriers. Urban metabolism (UM) provides an analytical foundation to address these challenges by conceptualising cities as dynamic systems of material, energy, water, and waste flows. By reframing NbS through a metabolic lens, this review highlights how UM can (i) generate operationally verifiable performance indicators, (ii) expose hidden material and energy flows underpinning NbS, (iii) quantify trade-offs in cost and energy use, and (iv) support the system-level integration of NbS with grey and hybrid infrastructures. We conclude by identifying research priorities for linking metabolic diagnostics with resilience indicators and governance mechanisms, thereby advancing the construction of adaptive and resource-efficient resilient cities.

title: Greenspace quality and proximity are stronger predictors of mental health than quantity or access
abstract: • Compared models of poor mental health with distinct urban greenspace characteristics. • Proxies for greenspace quality and proximity emerged as the strongest predictors. • Greenspace quantity and access were weaker in explaining variation in mental health. • Findings highlight the need to prioritise urban greenspace quality and proximity. As evidence grows for the mental health benefits of urban greenspaces, understanding which specific characteristics matter most is critical for guiding effective urban design and policy. This study compares multiple measures of greenspace exposure–focusing on proximity, quantity, access and quality–to determine which best predict changes in mental health. Individual-level mental health data were obtained from a nationally representative longitudinal survey in Great Britain (British Household Panel Survey, 1991–2008). The sample was restricted to individuals who moved neighbourhoods ( n = 492), and a Before-After-Control-Intervention (BACI) study design was applied. Individual repeated measures from before and after the move were used to quantify the effects of changes in greenspace exposure on the probability of poor mental health, here defined using GHQ-12 with a score ≥ 3. Generalised linear mixed models were developed and their relative performance compared to identify the best-performing models. Among seven models tested, models incorporating local bird species richness (proxy for greenspace quality) and proximity to local public greenspace provided the best fit, outperforming models based on quantity and access. To our knowledge, this is the first study to compare the effect of multiple greenspace measures on mental health using a BACI design specifically within an urban context. Our findings suggest the potential importance of urban greenspace quality and proximity in shaping mental health outcomes compared to measures of quantity and access. However, these findings are caveated by a temporal disconnect between exposure and outcome data; we therefore recommend that future studies validate these findings using temporally-aligned data. Based on this study’s findings, we recommend that future environmental planning and public health strategies prioritise these characteristics to maximise the mental health benefits of urban greenspaces.

title: Dual carbon-sink pathways of urban parks: linking direct carbon sequestration with indirect emission reduction
Changing landscapes and their effects on non-material benefits: challenges and opportunities for landscape science
abstract: Landscape changes are occurring at unprecedented rate and pace, affecting non-material benefits of human-nature interactions and highlighting the need for better integration of perceptions into decision-making. However, links between landscape changes and impacts on non-material benefits remain poorly understood, despite being core topics in landscape science. This paper aims to provide insights into current approaches to assess landscape changes and related impacts on non-material benefits, highlighting limitations and challenges of research in landscape science. In an interactive workshop setting, experts in landscape science collected and discussed assessment approaches to capture impacts on non-material benefits due to landscape changes as well as factors influencing perceptions of these changes. Current challenges and opportunities of research in landscape science are pointed out applying a Strengths–Weaknesses–Opportunities–Threats (SWOT) analysis. While landscape science as an interdisciplinary and increasingly transdisciplinary research field enables the holistic assessment of human-nature interactions and impacts from landscape changes on non-material benefits, conceptual and methodological issues limit knowledge production and hamper the integration into landscape planning and decision-making. Factors influencing perception of changes are still insufficiently understood, while technological developments can help to develop novel integrative methods. Landscape science has the potential to holistically assess the impacts on human-nature interactions caused by landscapes changes. However, there are several challenges and limitations that still need to be addressed, requiring a steady exchange between research and governance, as well as a better integration of the perception of diverse types of users and beneficiaries.

title: From government to governance? Investigating municipality-led steering in urban forestry: the case of the Amsterdamse Bos, The Netherlands
abstract: Successfully establishing and managing urban forests require governance modes that create enabling environments for the provision of societal benefits. While recent scholarship has increasingly focused on how public institutions rely on collaborative governance arrangements to achieve desired outcomes, less attention has been paid to the dynamics under which municipalities retain power over their urban forests, particularly in times of growing austerity and increasing demands for inclusiveness. This explanatory study addresses this gap by analyzing municipality-led urban forest governance, with the aim of deepening understanding of actors involved, narratives, resource allocation, processes, and power distribution shaping hierarchical approaches in urban forestry. Adopting a qualitative research design, this research analyses the governance characterizing the case of the Amsterdamse Bos , a peri -urban woodland located on the southern edge of Amsterdam. Adopting the Policy Arrangement Approach as analytical lens, findings show that over time the Municipality of Amsterdam has maintained a hierarchical model, supported by consolidated land tenure, political commitment, and resource mobilization capacity. This has secured actors coordination, policy discourse coherence, and the achievement of socio-economic and environmental management objectives. At the same time, the concentration of decision-making authority has entrenched power asymmetries, constrained intermunicipal collaboration, and limited opportunities for inclusive participation, with less powerful actors confined to operational rather than strategic roles. The study highlights both the advantages and limitations of municipality-led urban forest governance, suggesting that while hierarchical arrangements can ensure continuity and coherence, more equitable outcomes require combining municipal steering with mechanisms for shared vision-building.

title: Research note: a transferable entropy-centrality method for urban stability analysis
abstract: This Research Note presents a proof-of-concept methodology for evaluating urban stability by integrating entropy with a novel graph-based centrality measure. We propose the HA2/P index, where the squared convex hull area of a street segment’s reachable zone is divided by its perimeter, capturing both extent and compactness of accessibility. Weighted by indicators such as building area, population, greenery, and water, this index was calculated for every street segment across Lithuania using the sDNA toolbox and ArcGIS Pro. Shannon entropy was then applied to the distribution of values within 400-m hexagons, producing a composite “stability index” that balances configurational diversity and structural coherence. Results show that historical and multifunctional cores demonstrate high stability, while fragmented or monofunctional modernist areas display low stability. This method, transferable to different contexts, offers a scalable tool for detecting resilient, multifunctional urban structures and contributes to international debates on sustainable urban form and the 15-Minute City.

title: Editorial Board
Treeless streets and sleepless nights: How cities overprotect infrastructure and underprotect citizens
abstract: Urban landscapes must provide residents with a range of infrastructure, both grey and green. However, current regimes of risk management for utilities and transport infrastructure tend to prohibit the planting of trees and other greenery within fairly large distances of cables, pipes, hydrants and poles, among other features. This precautionary approach has sought to mitigate minor risks such as root intrusions, but has inadvertently had the cumulative effect of making significant areas of the public realm ‘leafless’. This exclusion of nature exposes residents to an array of quite serious health risks, which we outline. Drawing on medical evidence, contemporary examples and a narrative of lived experience, we argue that this is a badly imbalanced regime of risk management. This perspective illuminates the unintended health and social consequences of risk-averse infrastructure policies and advocates resilience-based approaches to urban tree integration, which will require significant reform to governance structures.

title: Increasing biodiversity and ecosystem functions along an age gradient of urban greenspaces
abstract: • Urban greenspace soils show substantial ecological development over time, despite persistent urban constraints. • Soil organic matter is a key indicator of development and encourages diverse, complex microbial communities. • Shifts in microbial communities enhance potential metabolic activity and traits, aligning with natural ecosystems. • Management should prioritize long-term ecological health and soil organic matter over short-term aesthetics. Urban greenspaces are constructed on soils disturbed by human activities, raising concerns about their capacity to sustain biodiversity and ecosystem functions. Uncertainty over whether these soils can recover toward conditions observed in natural ecosystems, as well as over the rates, mechanisms, and limits of soil development, has reinforced the perception that urban soils are irreversibly degraded. Here, we examined soil properties, microbial communities, and functional attributes across 30 urban greenspace sites spanning an age gradient in Seoul, Republic of Korea, using nearby natural ecosystems as references. Soil conditions improved with greenspace age, reflected in the accumulation of soil organic matter. These improvements were associated with higher microbial diversity and microbial gene copy numbers, along with increased potential metabolic capacity and shifts in functional attributes. Older sites harbored more plant-associated microbes and complex carbon decomposers, whereas taxa associated with pathogens and pollutants declined. Functional profiles showed increased ectomycorrhizal and saprotrophic functions, together with a broader potential for carbon metabolism in older sites. These findings identify soil organic matter as a key driver of ecological development in urban greenspaces and underscore the need to shift management from short-term, aesthetic-focused maintenance toward long-term strategies that enhance and maintain soil organic matter to support ecosystem services and resilience.

title: Greenness may increase ozone-related mortality risk via BVOC emissions: A WRF-CMAQ modeling and population-based study
Urban agriculture as an interface for policy–practice integration: a landscape-informed, multi-layer framework across Havana, New York city and Chongming Island
abstract: Urban agriculture is increasingly recognized as a multifunctional lever for urban sustainability, yet the mechanisms through which planning policies enable or constrain its integration into city systems remain poorly understood. This gap limits the development of evidence-based frameworks that can bridge policy intent and implementation practice. This study develops a transparent, multilingual content-analysis pipeline and a landscape-informed coupling framework to evaluate urban agriculture policy–practice alignment across three contrasting governance contexts: Havana (Cuba), New York City (USA), and Chongming Island (China). Using a PRISMA-ScR literature synthesis (n = 3145), we construct a five-domain, 40-keyword evaluation matrix and apply it to official policy corpora and flagship project documentation. Results show that human-centered approaches effectively translate social equity and food-provisioning aims but exhibit limited spatial integration; nature-based approaches advance ecological and morphological targets but underperform on participation; and the landscape-informed model achieves more balanced alignment across all five domains, though gaps persist in inter-layer connectivity. Situating these findings within the broader discourse on urban sustainability governance, we propose a multi-layered landscape framework spanning ecological, institutional, social, and spatial dimensions. This framework offers planners a structured diagnostic and prescriptive tool for embedding urban agriculture into integrated urban transitions.

title: Transmission corridors as multifunctional landscapes: New vision and transdisciplinary approaches to shape energy futures
abstract: Electricity transmission corridors are among the most extensive linear infrastructures shaping contemporary landscapes, yet they are typically managed as single-purpose technical spaces focused primarily on grid reliability and vegetation clearance. Despite their vast spatial footprint, their broader landscape potential remains largely overlooked in planning and design scholarship. This perspective article addresses this gap by advancing a transdisciplinary framework that conceptualizes transmission rights-of-way as multifunctional landscape systems capable of supporting community recreation, ecological restoration, and climate-adaptive land management. Drawing on literature across landscape planning, infrastructure governance, and conservation science, the article examines corridor opportunities through three complementary lenses: recreation and public access, biodiversity-oriented vegetation management, and fire-adaptive landscape design. As wildfire risks intensify across many regions, proactive and integrated fuels management within transmission corridors can reduce ignition and fire spread while simultaneously supporting regional recreation networks and ecological connectivity at scale. International examples—including the Meadoway in Toronto, Canada, the ELIA LIFE + Biodiversity project in Belgium and France, the Ecological Energy Network in the Netherlands, and emerging fire-adaptive corridor design cases in the United States and China—illustrate how coordinated planning, integrated vegetation management, and cross-sector partnerships can transform transmission rights-of-way into community greenways, ecological networks, and strategic landscape buffers. By positioning transmission corridors as multifunctional landscapes, this article highlights how landscape planning and design can help guide the spatial governance, ecological performance, and public value of future energy landscapes.

title: Native carnivores decline along rural–urban gradients dominated by dogs and cats
Trait-basis and environmental drivers of urban biotic homogenization: a temporal analysis in a subtropical megacity
abstract: Urbanization alters biodiversity not only by changing species richness but also by reshaping community composition. Biotic homogenization represents a major and debated potential outcome of compositional changes in urban communities. However, owing to the lack of temporal data, the current understanding of its occurrence and underlying mechanisms remains limited. Here, based on three periods of field survey (2005, 2017, and 2023) of 104 transects across the urbanization gradient in Guangzhou, a southern Chinese megacity, we investigated the spatiotemporal changes in avian alpha, beta and gamma diversity. Particularly, we partitioned the temporal dynamics of beta diversity to explore mechanisms of compositional changes in the avian community. We assessed the associations between species contributions to temporal changes in beta diversity and their functional traits while also examining the effects of environmental changes on synchronous changes in beta diversity. We found that, across all urbanization gradients, the average alpha diversity of the transects increased remarkably between 2005 and 2023, while beta diversity exhibited a concomitant decline. This decline in beta diversity was primarily driven by the widespread colonization of species with traits such as wider distribution ranges, higher hand-wing indices, and larger clutch sizes. Gross domestic productivity (GDP) and human population density emerged as the primary environmental drivers of temporal changes in beta diversity. The results provide direct empirical evidence to support the contentious urban biotic homogenization hypothesis. These findings warn that an exclusive emphasis on enhancing local species richness may lead urban managers to overlook the risk of compositional homogenization in urban communities at the regional scale. Therefore, long-term monitoring of urban biodiversity is crucial for accurately assessing the ecological consequences of urbanization and for developing more targeted conservation measures.

title: Exploring Before-and-After visual preferences of street interventions using Google Street View time travel
abstract: • Developed a immersive, scalable survey using GSV Time-Machine for street preferences. • The tool enables temporal analysis using real panoramic images. • The tool follows the GSV Terms of Use being replicable for other applications. • Parents and non-experts show a higher preference for car-oriented interventions. • Support for active modes grows with experience; less impact seen for bus interventions. Urban spaces are changing in response to the current paradigm shift in mobility planning, which is moving away from car-oriented planning, prioritizing public transport and active modes. The decision-making process is shifting from a solely expert-led and politician-driven model to one that integrates citizens’ preferences and expectations, acknowledging the importance of a better understanding of public attitudes toward street design reconfigurations. Current research relies on resource-intensive and time-consuming experiments, rarely considering the element of change. Consequently, the main contribution of this work is the development of a visual stated preference survey methodology designed to evaluate individuals’ preferences regarding street interventions by comparing conditions before and after their implementation. The approach uses Google Street View’s ‘Time Machine’ feature to represent real-world changes, embedding iframe-based visualizations that enable pairwise comparisons between pre- and post-intervention scenarios. The visual stated preference survey was designed to capture preferences in different street interventions types focusing on prioritizing car, bus or active modes among diverse population groups. This framework not only ensures compliance with Google’s usage policies and is reproducible but also provides respondents with an immersive 360-degree environment that allow a more complete visualization of the transformations on the street. Although the survey was disseminated world-wide, respondents primarily resided in Portugal (53.2%) and had an urban planning background (54.8%). The methodological contribution is reproducible, scalable, and can be deployed across diverse geographic contexts, helping to mitigate current sampling limitations in future applications. Although the results are not generalizable to all contexts, car-oriented interventions had the lowest preference rate, and parents and nonexperts showed comparatively higher support for these interventions. These group effects were not observed in active-modes-oriented interventions, which had a near-unanimous preference for the ”after” scenarios. Bus-oriented interventions received a more moderate level of support. In particular, suburban residents consistently preferred all types of transitions. Results highlight the importance of inclusive consultation and tailored communication strategies to address the difference in perceptions of specific groups.

title: Children’s playgrounds as potential habitats for urban pollinators: Floral abundance matters
abstract: • Children’s playgrounds support less pollinators compared to neighbouring green areas. • Pollinators in playgrounds are strongly associated to local floral abundance. • Best children’s playgrounds hosted more individuals and species than control sites. • Bees were abundant in early summer, while bumblebees and butterflies in late summer. • Honeybee abundance was negatively associated with solitary bee abundance in early summer. Urbanisation is a key driver of pollinator declines, yet the ecological potential of unconventional urban habitats remains poorly understood. Among these, children’s playgrounds are ubiquitous but virtually unstudied urban green spaces. We conducted the first systematic assessment of playgrounds as pollinator habitats in Prague, Czech Republic, by comparing pollinator communities in playgrounds and paired control sites (parks and urban lawns). In a two-year study, we sampled honeybees and wild bees (excluding bumblebees) at 82 sites and bumblebees and butterflies in more than 60 sites in early and late summer using standardised netting and visual transects. Simultaneously, we assessed local habitat characteristics (vegetation, floral abundance, bare ground, shade, and impervious surfaces) and surrounding landscape composition. Across taxa, playgrounds supported significantly fewer species and individuals than nearby green spaces, a pattern consistent across years and seasons. However, floral abundance was the most important predictor of species richness and abundance, with stronger effects in playgrounds, where even small floral increases yielded disproportionately high pollinator gains. In contrast, other local variables and landscape composition showed little or no influence. Moreover, we detected negative associations between honeybee and wild bee abundance in the early season within control sites, indicating potential competition for floral resources with this group but not with other pollinators. These findings demonstrate that playgrounds are currently suboptimal habitats but hold substantial potential, as some playgrounds in our dataset outperformed neighbouring control sites. Enhancing floral resources alone could rapidly increase their ecological value and transform them into contributors to urban biodiversity.

How Recognitional Justice (Re)Shapes Access and Participation in Urban Green Space Governance
abstract: Urban Green Space (UGS) policy has mostly focused either on addressing the distributional inequities and subsequent levels of access, or procedural inequities to widen public participation in their governance. In this paper, we build on work focussing on recognitional equity – a dimension of equity which calls for the acknowledgement and respect of diverse identities, values, and experiences – to deepen understandings of existing UGS inequalities. We develop an analytical framework that highlights how recognitional justice relates to both access and governance of UGS to explore UGS equity in Oxford, one of the most unequal cities in the UK. Using a mixed-method approach, we provide a spatial analysis of the available green space and relative influencing factors for three neighbourhoods with differing socio-economic deprivation levels and local planning provisions. Qualitatively, we consider with community members their values underpinning access to UGS, and their ability and willingness to participate in local governance. Overall, we show how recognitional injustices impact different socio-economic groups based on existing procedural and distributional inequities, making local UGS more vulnerable to loss in neighbourhoods that are relatively bioculturally diverse and socio-economically deprived. Ongoing institutional failures to account for principles of recognitional justice and embed strategies to mitigate the uneven impacts of system-embedded inequities risk continued erosion, rather than improvement, of UGS justice for the most deprived.

Risk assessment in the Pyrocene – Rapid changes in models and predictions complicate US policies to prioritize forest and fuel management
abstract: Increased wildfire activity in the US motivated the USDA Forest Service to update national wildfire simulation data used for risk assessment and prioritizing wildland fuel reduction programs. The update (FSim-2020 to FSim-2023) included revised data on fuels, ignition frequency, fire weather, and recalibration of the FSim model. We overlayed the new simulated fire perimeters with the most recent building footprint data to examine the change in magnitude and spatial patterns of estimated building exposure. We found that the update to FSim-2023 resulted in a 61% increase in simulated building exposure in the East, and a decline of −9% in the West compared to FSim-2020. Overall, Forest Service priorities for management investments at the 100,000-ha scale were consistent between the two simulations in the West, but less so for the East, with newer simulations suggesting that a substantially greater area would require treatments to address the same level of exposure. Fire return level analysis indicated that differences between the prior and newer simulated building exposure varied across predicted recurrence intervals and fire size. Changes in building exposure were related to increases in ignition frequency, burn probability and building counts. A potentially important finding was the overestimation of simulated building exposure compared with observed (+112% West, +790% East) for the same approximate time period. One probable cause for the overestimation was the resampling of the LANDFIRE 30 m to the FSim 270 m, which resulted in a substantial reclassification of non-burnable to burnable pixels, particularly in and around the urban interface. The study underscores the importance of continued federal investment in risk assessment technology and data to keep pace with the rapid growth in wildfire extent and severity under evolving wildfire management policy.

title: How can urban tree protection policies be more effective? Exploring landowners’ experience of a tree protection mechanism on private land
abstract: Should governments intervene more to protect trees on private urban land? If so, how? Despite the many benefits of urban trees for citizens’ well-being, biodiversity and climate change mitigation, maintaining and increasing urban canopy cover on private land can be difficult. Tree protection policies often involve interference with private land rights. The views of impacted private landowners can add valuable information to the current knowledge on improving tree protection policies. This research explores the impacts of one form of tree protection policy on private landowners. I interviewed 19 Australian landowners that had one or more trees on their land protected by a tree registration mechanism, seeking insights into participants’ reported experience of the effects of the tree protection mechanism, and how participants believe this mechanism could be improved. Landowners expressed pride in their trees, and found the tree register to be of benefit in resolving neighbour disputes over the tree. Assistance in the form of reduced local government taxes was a common suggestion from landowners, not only to help with maintenance costs but also to signify recognition of the tree’s value to the community. Arborists’ advice was also highly valued by landowners to alleviate concerns about limb drop. Landowners felt that government provision of broad-reaching education about trees would bolster community support for tree protection. Landowners acknowledged a tension between the rights of the individual over private land and the needs of the community.

title: The hedonic value of urban greenspaces: A three-level meta-analysis across the globe
abstract: Urban greenspaces (UGS) contribute to residential property values, and their hedonic effects have been evaluated using Hedonic Price Modelling (HPM) approach. Yet, systematic synthesis of UGS hedonic effects remains limited. This meta-analysis aims to fill in this knowledge gap. A total of 228 observations from 88 primary studies spanning North America, Europe, Asia and Australia are taken into a three-level random-effects meta-regression model, to synthesize the hedonic impacts of UGS attributes (including type, availability, proximity, and visibility) while addressing methodological and contextual variation. The modelling results reveal several key factors in explaining the heterogeneity of UGS hedonic values across varying spatial scales. At the global level, while positive values prevail, several negative effects have been reported. UGS proximity and specific types contribute positively to effect sizes, UGS availability would reduce the magnitude of effect sizes. Interestingly UGS visibility is insignificantly associated with effect sizes. At the regional level, UGS proximity is consistently valued, and visibility is consistently insignificant. Substantial geographical heterogeneity also emerged, Asian and European homebuyers pay little attention to UGS type and availability, respectively. Taking spatial effects into account could significantly reduce effect size, mainly due to the amelioration of potential biases attributed to complex spatial interactions within housing markets. Regarding ancillary variables included in global and regional meta-analyses, adopting spatial modelling is negatively associated with effect sizes, which is particularly important for empirical studies in Asian cities, likely attributed to the dominance of apartment buildings in housing markets and associated complex spatial interactions. Additionally, population density is statistically important for empirical studies in North American, suggesting that homebuyers value UGS more where population density in higher. These findings confirm the significance of UGS hedonic value in residential housing market globally and the heterogeneous premiums attached to specific UGS attributes across different regions, which could help refine HPM studies considering UGS attributes and modelling options to adequately capture homebuyers’ preferences for and UGS hedonic premiums. Hence, accurate estimation of UGS hedonic value can be generated to inform urban planning strategies.

title: Spatio-temporal access to protected areas from Australian significant urban areas
abstract: There are many positive effects of the natural environment on human health and wellbeing. These benefits are closely linked to people’s accessibility to protected areas like National Parks. In this study, we quantified spatial and temporal relationships between the extent of protected areas in, and adjacent to, significant urban areas (SUAs) in Australia, the populations of SUAs, and the network service area of connecting SUAs with protected areas between 2001 and 2024. To evaluate the accessibility of SUAs to protected areas, we developed a gravity-based accessibility index using a network analysis approach. The Gravity Index is a relative measure of attractiveness of a protected area in terms of the distance that needs to be travelled to access it, and the level of possible “congestion” placed on it from the population of the surrounding network service area. SUAs with a high value for the Gravity Index reflect shorter distances to travel to protected areas, along with fewer people per unit of area visiting protected areas (low congestion). Our results reveal marked differences in the Gravity Index for SUAs across Australia. Some SUAs, such as Hobart and Canberra, were characterized by a comparatively high Gravity Index, indicating extensive protected areas within a short distance of those population centres. Others, such as Melbourne (Australia’s fastest growing SUA), had a very low and declining Gravity Index, associated with high population growth (1.8 million in 24 years), small fragmented existing protected areas surrounding the city, and limited additional land added to the protected area network over the period of population growth. Our results identify priority SUAs (such as Melbourne) where there is a need to expand the protected area network through, for example, changing land tenures to National Parks.

title: Linking street-level greenery to environmental microbial diversity: A multiscalar analysis in the Taipei metropolitan area
abstract: Urbanization has led to a significant reduction in green spaces, altering microbial habitats and potentially contributing to the growing prevalence of immune-mediated diseases. Urban greenery may serve as a reservoir for more diverse environmental microbiota, yet the links between street-level vegetation and environmental microbial diversity remain poorly understood. This study investigates how the visibility of greenery, measured through the Green View Index (GVI), relates to microbial richness and Shannon’s diversity across urban habitat gradients in the Taipei metropolitan area. Environmental DNA samples and Google Street View panoramas for calculating GVI were collected from three sublocation types: biodiversity hotspots featuring urban green spaces, residential building entrances, and pavements linking biodiversity hotspots and entrances. Our findings show that biodiversity hotspots support greater microbial diversity, and significant GVI–microbial correlations occur only in biodiversity hotspots, not in pavements or entrances. This positive correlation observed in biodiversity hotspots suggests that street-level vegetation can reflect the diversity of environmental microbial communities. These results highlight the importance of incorporating green infrastructure into urban planning to enhance microbial habitat heterogeneity and promote microbial diversity. As urbanization continues to sever citizens’ contact with nature, this initiative helps maintain the environmental microbiota essential for immune regulation and support public health. Future research should incorporate longitudinal and cross-seasonal studies to evaluate the durability of GVI-microbial relationships, examine the influence of vegetation types and structural complexity, and explore how urban greenery can act both as a scientific indicator and a public engagement tool in biodiversity-aware urban design.

title: Expanding protected areas for biodiversity and ecosystem services considering climate change: A case of the Yangtze River Economic Belt in China
Discursive coalitions and environmental justice: Empty signifiers in green and blue infrastructure planning in Girona, Spain
abstract: This article examines how discursive coalitions compete to define green and blue infrastructure (GBI) in Girona, a mid-sized Mediterranean city in Spain, and the extent to which they engage with ideas of environmental justice (EJ). Drawing on critical discourse analysis of 23 semi-structured interviews and municipal planning documents linked to three emblematic GBI initiatives, we identified three discursive coalitions. Green Capitalism frames GBI as a vehicle for economic growth, place branding, and funding acquisition. Commons emphasizes collective stewardship, social cohesion, and redistributive claims. Technical prioritizes expert-led planning and management efficiency. We show that coalitions compete to stabilize meanings around contested terms such as nature, resilience, and wellbeing, which operate as empty signifiers, flexible labels whose meaning depends on discursive context and around which divergent policy imaginaries are articulated. Green Capitalism is most prominent in institutional agendas, where EU funding logics shape priorities and accelerate grant-fitting project design. Commons actors contest these trajectories, foregrounding distributive justice concerns and demanding meaningful participation and recognition. Technical actors support ecological objectives but often translate justice into universal access and efficiency, which can depoliticise trade-offs and narrow recognitional and procedural commitments. The findings illustrate how discursive formations condition policy trajectories, institutional logics, and the political space available for justice-oriented interventions. Theoretically, this study advances discourse-based approaches to EJ through the operationalization of discursive hegemony in urban greening. Empirically, it contributes to the growing body of EJ research in mid-sized cities, illustrating how discursive struggles in these settings can bolster or inhibit socially just urban transformations.

title: Exploring rewilding as a potential design approach to improve urban biodiversity: A systematic review of the literature
abstract: Urban biodiversity continues to decline under rapid urbanization. Although biophilic design and green–blue infrastructure have strengthened nature integration into cities, planning and design practice often prioritizes human-centered service delivery and overlooks process-led recovery. Rewilding addresses this gap by foregrounding ecological autonomy, succession, and trophic complexity, yet its urban translation remains limited. This review therefore examined how rewilding could be operationalized as a design-oriented strategy in cities. An evidence-to-design roadmap was proposed to link rewilding logics, biodiversity aims, and urban planning and design, with a dual-level protocol adopted: 1) a macro-level scientometric overview of 1184 records (1990–2025) to locate urban rewilding studies within the broader literature; and 2) a micro-level PRISMA-guided synthesis of 103 spatially explicit studies coded by rewilding pathway (active/passive), targets, spatial and temporal scales, data, methods, and spatial variables. Macro mapping indicated that urban-related studies were late-emerging and weakly consolidated. Micro synthesis revealed pathway differences: passive studies primarily traced vegetation and landscape trajectories, while active studies employed suitability and connectivity modeling for intervention screening. Urban studies remained scarce (N = 9), with passive studies dominant and connectivity analyses particularly common, focusing on vegetation, birds, and planning-oriented targets. Building on these patterns, this study derived a four-level framework comprising design intent, strategic planning, tactical methodology, and operational application, translating rewilding into staged, scalable decisions aligned with urban planning and design workflows. This review positioned rewilding as a process-centered complement to conventional landscape design approaches, offering an actionable pathway for embedding biodiversity regeneration within urban systems.

title: Exploring the impact of map uncertainty on soil sealing versus conservation decisions
abstract: Incorporating soil quality into land-planning decisions is considered a crucial initial step in minimizing the environmental and human well-being impacts of soil sealing. In recent years, land planners have gained greater access to soil quality maps and, in the best cases, to their associated uncertainty. However, it remains unclear how the representation of map uncertainty influences decision-making, and how this influence varies depending on the decision to be made (conservation/conversion) and land-planners’ backgrounds or socio-demographic characteristics. This paper presents the results of a map-based survey, in which respondents were shown soil quality maps with varying levels and representations of uncertainty, and asked to make either sealing or conservation decisions. We determined through a statistical analysis how the different factors (level of uncertainty, map resolution, type of visualization, self reported comfort, expertise, etc.) influence decision-making, and how their influence varies across decision scenarios (sealing vs. conservation). We showed that the main factors at play are soil quality and uncertainty level. Their effects, however, depend on the decision scenario. We also demonstrated that end-users were able to incorporate uncertainty information into their decisions, and quantified, in each scenario, the threshold above which uncertainty impedes decision-making. These results highlight the impact of map uncertainty on planners’ decisions and underline the need for clear representation, as many environmental maps used in land planning are inherently uncertain.

title: How elevated-road design and adjacent building configuration shape vertical exposure to traffic-related particles in dense urban environments
Perceptions of rewilding in European abandoned agricultural lands
abstract: Agricultural abandonment has been a trend in Europe over recent decades. The resultant abandoned land has been faced with multiple land change trajectories, including rewilding processes. Rewilding aims at facilitating ecological recovery, often through the reduction of human influence on the landscape or through restoring trophic complexity. However, rewilding is not always welcomed as it can challenge the place attachment stakeholders have for pre-existing and current landscapes. A total of 80 articles, published within Europe between 2000 and 2024, were analysed and coded using a conceptual framework. We found that the body of literature describing rewilding-related preferences is heterogeneous, with rewilding often being an implicit concept rather than an umbrella term encompassing related processes. Proforestation, the rewilding of forest areas, was rarely addressed in the literature, and while case-studies were found throughout the continent, they were under-represented in Eastern Europe, specifically in agricultural abandonment hotspots of the Carpathians and Baltic regions. Rather than rewilding, traditional management of the landscape was often preferred, specifically by rural, older, and farming communities. Discontent towards rewilding was primarily related to concerns around its potential impacts over the landscape such as landscape homogenisation and on economic activities within the area such as food production. The literature shows agreement on the need for better alignment between actors’ perspectives and rewilding objectives relying on stakeholder engagement, trust building, and financial support. Attention should be given to the evolution of perceptions, specifically given the dynamic nature of rewilding processes and the influence of knowledge and experiences on preferences.
