Urban ponds as nature-based solutions for heat mitigation and temperature regulation in highly urbanised regions
abstract: Understanding of the role of urban blue spaces in mitigating heat risks is increasingly important as the climate changes, cities densify and the urban population, and ages, all of which heighten population exposure to extreme heat. Although urban ponds and other water bodies are a common feature of many cities, changes in the quantity, areal extent and cooling ability of urban ponds and subsequent implications for heat exposure are rarely explored. We examined this issue in the East Harima region of Japan, where urbanisation and industrialisation have progressed in recent years, using remote sensing imagery from early summer in 1985 and 2022 and spatial statistical analysis. Urban expansion increased impervious surfaces, while water bodies and forested areas decreased. The number and patch size of urban ponds decreased, but changes in their cooling effect varied. Of 337 ponds identified in 1985, 306 (90.80%) provided cooling effects. Average cooling was 2.95 °C and the mean cooling effect was 0.0230 °C/m. Of 274 ponds that remained in 2022, 206 (75.18%) provided cooling effects. Average cooling was 3.70 °C and mean cooling was 0.01855 °C/m. In central areas, the thermal gradient between water bodies and impervious surfaces enhanced the cooling effect due to an increase in buildings and reduction of green spaces. However, pond fragmentation or disappearance and installation of floating solar panels undermined cooling, turning ponds into local surface heat islands. These findings demonstrate that small urban ponds which are meaningful to urban heat mitigation, particularly in densely populated areas. Where pond quantity and size remain constant, and the density of impervious surfaces increases, cooling benefits derived from these urban blue spaces can increase. However, increased impervious surfaces often accompany pond deterioration. Further research is needed to fully understand and maximise the potential of urban ponds in enhancing urban resilience.

title: Aligning green spaces with human activity: uncovering opportunity-realization mismatches in urban green exposure
abstract: Urban green exposure provides multiple benefits, but its effectiveness depends not only on the presence of green spaces but also on whether such opportunities are realized through residents’ daily activities. However, existing assessments largely emphasize exposure opportunities and provide limited diagnosis of opportunity–realization mismatches at life-circle scale. This study developed a 15-min life-circle based opportunity–realization framework in which passive green exposure (PGE) represents exposure opportunities and human activity green exposure (HAGE), constructed by integrating location-based service (LBS) data into PGE assessment, represents realized exposure. Using 2966 life-circle service areas in Shanghai, this study quantified HAGE and PGE across visibility, availability, and accessibility pathways, identified mismatch clusters using local bivariate Moran’s I, and applied an XGBoost–GeoShapley model to assess landscape configuration associations. Results showed that 911 service areas (30.7%) exhibited significant mismatches, revealing substantial local decoupling between green exposure opportunities and realization. These mismatches comprised two distinct regimes: high-realization/low-opportunity (HL), reflecting concentrated realization under limited or weakly embedded opportunities, and low-realization/high-opportunity (LH), reflecting inefficient conversion of existing opportunities into realized exposure. GeoShapley results further suggest differentiated planning implications: HL mitigation should expand and embed effective exposure opportunities by improving green space boundary and interface conditions and green contact along residents’ mobility routes. LH mitigation should activate existing green spaces by enhancing entrances, route integration, and attractiveness. Overall, this study provides a quantitative diagnostic framework to support more targeted planning for urban green exposure opportunity–realization mismatches.

title: Co-designing urban soundscapes with citizens and experts: Evidence from a field experiment
abstract: The growing role of expert input in participatory environmental planning and design has raised concerns about citizen voice. However, there remains limited causal evidence on how expert input, combined with public involvement, influences deliberation and trust. We address this democratic tension through a citizen–driven soundscape co-design experiment embedded in a soundscape investigation in central London. In this work, participants were presented with a range of aural–visual scenarios, including emerging acoustic–metamaterial (AMM) and acoustic–wall interventions for a public space, and collaboratively generated 144 alternative soundscape proposals. We evaluated these proposals using the Soundscape Perception Index (SPI) against ‘Vibrant’ and ‘Calm’ targets to assess how group deliberation and expert input affect design performance. We found that the designs created by citizens in groups consistently outperformed those developed individually, highlighting the value of group deliberation in participatory soundscape design. Structured expert input further improved group outcomes, particularly for the more challenging ‘Calm’ target, while showing minimal influence on individual designs. These findings suggest that expert contributions are most effective when embedded in a partnership model that promotes citizen agency. Building on these insights, we propose an SPI-based, engineering-informed evaluation framework for participatory soundscape design that makes the effects of participatory process conditions on design outcomes measurable and comparable while transparently integrating expertise with citizen deliberation.

title: A multi-scale identification and optimization framework of ecological sources for different conservation objectives
Intensifying drought threatens the heat-regulating capacity of urban vegetation
abstract: Urban vegetation is critical in regulating urban heat, yet the stability of this regulatory effect under drought has not been well measured at a global scale. Using satellite observations during 2003–2024 across 2911 cities, we found that vegetation greening reduced urban land surface temperature (LST) with the strongest global mean daytime reduction of 0.405°C in summer and the weakest of 0.066°C in winter. Nighttime effects were weaker, averaging 0.049°C in summer and 0.008°C in winter. Critically, vegetation-related cooling exhibited pronounced nonlinear and threshold-limited responses to drought. During daytime in spring, summer, and autumn, cooling was generally stronger under wetter conditions but declined after crossing drought thresholds, occurring at Palmer Drought Severity Index (PDSI) values of −0.925, −0.827, and −0.754, respectively. Beyond these thresholds, cooling declined rapidly, with the drought-cooling relationship shifting from positive to negative, and the steepest post-threshold change observed in summer, where the slope changed from 0.201 to −0.205°C per unit PDSI. At night, threshold responses also occurred but with weaker magnitudes, with PDSI thresholds ranging from −0.943 in spring to −2.057 in winter. Statistical pathway analysis showed that drought-LST associations shifted across thresholds, consistent with expected drought-related changes in estimated evapotranspiration and constrained by vegetation shading and seasonal radiation-moisture conditions. Together, these results demonstrate that the heat-regulating capacity of urban vegetation is not linear or unlimited, but constrained by interacting water and energy conditions. This highlights the need for awareness of thresholds and water-constraints when using urban vegetation to mitigate warming temperatures under climate change.

title: Mobilising nature-based solutions (NbS) for coastal protection: Public preferences for hard, soft and hybrid coastal protection measures in Bali, Indonesia
abstract: Mobilising nature-based solutions (NbS) is increasingly considered as a sustainable and climate-resilient alternative to conventional approaches to coastal protection. This often involves trade-offs between protection effectiveness/timing, ecological outcomes, and infrastructure design that vary between contexts. However, public preferences regarding these trade-offs remain insufficiently understood, particularly in rapidly developing coastal regions in the Global South. This study aims to investigate public preferences of coastal protection measures focusing on Bali (Indonesia), a rapidly transforming and tourism-dependent coastal region facing increasing climate and development pressures. We employ a discrete choice experiment (DCE) (n = 370) analysed using a Mixed Logit model and Latent Class Analysis (LCA) to evaluate how trade-offs in key attributes of coastal protection measures (“Protection level”, “Urgency of protection”, “Lifetime”, “Biodiversity” and “Materials) influence public choices across very different coastal protection paradigms (hard, soft, and hybrid measures), and the related heterogeneity. The results reveal strong preference for coastal protection options characterised by full protection, faster implementation, longer durability, natural materials, and positive impacts on biodiversity. Among the alternatives, hybrid measures were the most preferred, followed by hard and soft measures. However, there is significant heterogeneity in preferences across socio-demographic characteristics. By explicitly examining trade-offs between the preferences for hard, hybrid, and soft coastal protection measures, we provide new empirical evidence on public support for multifunctional coastal protection approaches. This evidence fills to the growing literature on NbS by demonstrating how public preferences can inform the design of climate-resilient coastal protection strategies in tourism-dependent coastal regions and other rapidly developing coastal areas.

title: Observer-related factors and the perception of cultural ecosystem (dis)services
abstract: While Cultural Ecosystem Services (CES) are co-produced through interactions between people and nature, the specific individual factors that shape these perceptions remain poorly understood, limiting the ability to manage green spaces inclusively. To address this gap, this study applies a co-production framework to explore the relationship between different observer-related factors and the perception of CES benefits and ecosystem disservices (EDS). To provide a more comprehensive understanding, we consider multiple dimensions of these factors, including human capital (socio-demographics), cultural capital (values toward nature), and characteristics of interaction with nature (flow of CES). We surveyed 684 visitors across seven green spaces in the Małopolska Region (Poland), selected for their ecological and social diversity. Our findings reveal that the relationship between these factors and perceived CES benefits and EDS varies significantly based on the type of benefit/EDS. Benefits such as connection to nature, spirituality, physical regeneration, a sense of freedom, and support for others’ development were strongly associated with all three observer-related dimensions. In contrast, benefits like aesthetics, self-development, and a sense of belonging appeared largely universal and independent of these factors. EDS patterns also differed: fear, discomfort, and reluctance were linked to gender, while anger, irritation, and sadness correlated with visit frequency. These results highlight the importance of inclusive management to tailor green spaces to diverse user needs. We propose a dual approach combining infrastructural solutions with educational and co-creative interventions, providing a flexible framework adaptable to various governance contexts.

title: City landscape in sight: A crowdsourced framework for unlocking urban-scale window view perceptions from real estate imagery
abstract: City landscapes viewed through home windows influence quality of life, yet perceptions of actual window views at the urban scale remain understudied. This study presents an approach for large-scale mapping of perceptions using 12,334 window view images (WVIs) collected from actual residential properties listed on real estate platforms in Wuhan, China, representing a rarely explored form of urban view imagery that offers advantages over the rendered or simulated window views commonly examined in previous studies. Through a non-immersive virtual reality platform, we collected 27,477 pairwise comparisons across six perceptual dimensions (e.g. preference) from 304 participants based on 499 WVIs. A hybrid neural network model was trained to predict human perceptions of all crowdsourced WVIs and map their spatial distribution. Results reveal significant spatial autocorrelation with distinct hot and cold spots across the whole city. Floor level strongly influences human perceptions: while higher floors offer more preferred and extensive window views, lower-floor windows provide residents with quiet and vivid views. An inference model further shows that window view composition matters considerably: high ratios of sky, trees, and low-rise buildings enhance people's preferences and perceptions of vividness, whereas high ratios of high-rise buildings increase perceptions of monotony and oppression. Importantly, these effects are non-linear: the excessive presence of certain elements can alter their impact on human perception. This work advances urban-scale understanding of residents' visual experiences and offers a transferable, human-centric method to inform urban planning and design aimed at improving the visual quality of window views.

title: The paradox of tree canopies: nonlinearity and spatial non-stationarity of green view factor in mitigating urban heat island
Integrating multidimensional fragmentation assessment with precise spatial design to sustain urban mangrove landscapes
Blackbird movements and habitat selection inform restoration of functional connectivity across cities
abstract: Although ecological restoration strategies are increasingly promoted to enhance biodiversity, ecosystem services and climate resilience in cities, little is known about their impact on functional connectivity. We integrated empirical movement data with spatially explicit connectivity modelling to assess how alternative urban restoration strategies may affect breeding habitat availability and functional connectivity for the common blackbird ( Turdus merula ) in Gijón (NW Spain). Telemetry data from 13 adults were used to assess home range size, movement distances and habitat selection within the urban matrix. This dataset allowed to parameterise resistance surfaces and identify potential breeding habitat patches, which served as nodes in a circuit-theory-based connectivity framework. To evaluate how different urban restoration strategies may influence habitat availability and connectivity, we compared three scenarios representing increasing levels of restoration intensity. Under baseline conditions, suitable breeding habitat was highly fragmented. Although nearly 10% of the study area was suitable, only one third was functionally connected. The “Connectors Restoration” scenario, adding small-scale linear connectors along streets, was predicted to substantially improve connectivity among existing patches despite it did not increase habitat availability. The “Targeted Restoration” scenario, promoting strategically selected public green areas, was associated with the highest efficiency, achieving large gains in habitat availability and connectivity with relatively limited restoration effort. The “Full Restoration” of all public green infrastructure yielded the largest absolute gains, but showed lower efficiency, indicating diminishing marginal returns at broader spatial scales. Overall, our results suggest that connectivity-informed planning may enhance landscape functioning in dense urban environments and highlight the importance of targeted restoration actions to maximise ecological outcomes under limited resources.

title: Should I stay or should I go: How urban heat gradients affect the local distribution of birds and bats
abstract: Facing escalating biodiversity decline, threats extend beyond species loss to reduced evolutionary and functional potential in ecosystems. Urbanisation is one of the main causes of biodiversity loss, and its impact is expected to be further increased by the anticipated growth in the human population over the coming decades. In this context, achieving sustainable development requires a balance between conservation and urban growth. A key step in characterizing the impacts of urbanisation on biodiversity using integrative approaches that reflect current scenarios of global change. This study focuses on the main representatives of urban flying vertebrates, birds and bats, to study how different levels of urbanisation affect these components of biodiversity. More precisely, we examine the influence of Urban Heat Islands (UHIs), as a proxy of strong urbanisation, on community composition and taxonomic, phylogenetic and functional diversity of bats and birds in the French city of Poitiers. We also assess the contribution of turnover and nestedness to community composition. Our results indicate that high urbanisation, reflected by UHIs, affects community composition, particularly for bats, whose diversity across taxonomic, phylogenetic and functional components is reduced. In contrast, birds display only a decline in taxonomic diversity in these zones. Turnover is the dominant process structuring bird communities, whereas nestedness primarily drives bat assemblages, suggesting greater potential for species replacement in birds. These results highlight the differing vulnerability of birds and bats to urbanisation and emphasize the need to consider these differences and the ecological interactions between them in conservation and urban planning strategies.

Beyond scenic views: an integrative review of visual research on heritage landscapes—themes, methods, and typologies across scales
abstract: Visual landscape research on heritage landscapes has expanded rapidly since 1995, yet its themes, study objects, and methods remain dispersed across disciplinary traditions. This review synthesizes 203 peer-reviewed studies published between 1995 and 2025 using a three-layered analytical framework that combines thematic coding, VOSviewer-based keyword co-occurrence analysis, and exploratory cross-dimensional Sankey mapping. Thematic coding shows that the field is concentrated around analysis/evaluation and management/conservation themes, with study objects dominated by formally recognized and spatially bounded heritage landscapes and methods centered on perception-based empirical approaches, GIS-based analysis, digital documentation, mixed methods, and multi-criteria evaluation. Keyword co-occurrence and cross-dimensional mapping further show that these distributions are organized through recurring but uneven theme–object–method associations. Three gaps are especially evident: perceptual and spatial evidence are often weakly coupled; less formalized, everyday, hybrid, and cross-scalar heritage landscapes remain underrepresented; and visual evidence is inconsistently translated into assessment, planning, and management contexts. Based on these findings, the review develops a review-derived organizing synthesis that relates research themes, heritage landscape types and scales, and methodological approaches. This synthesis clarifies the current structure of visual heritage landscape research, identifies underexplored intersections, and provides a basis for more transparent comparison and future empirical work.

title: “Tire Operation” model: A disaster-driven hybrid framework for assessing ecological resilience and guiding spatial planning in hazard-prone communities
abstract: Community ecosystems are increasingly vulnerable to disturbance risks due to climate change and intensified natural hazards. Existing research on ecological resilience has primarily focused on macro-scale social systems, often overlooking the interaction between disaster processes and ecological responses at the community level. This study proposes a hybrid ecological resilience assessment framework—referred to as the “Tire Operation”—based on three core capacities: ecosystem base robustness (EBR), ecosystem disaster adaptability (EDA), and ecosystem restoration potential (ERP). The assessment framework integrates ecological components (elements, structure, function) with disaster processes (pressure, state, response) to evaluate community ecological resilience across spatial and temporal scales. Using debris flow-prone communities in western Sichuan, China, the study integrates habitat quality modelling (InVEST), ecological carrying capacity analysis, ecosystem service valuation, machine learning (XGBoost), and debris flow dynamics simulation to assess resilience under a centennial disaster scenario. Results reveal pronounced spatial heterogeneity and nonlinear interactions among EBR, EDA, and ERP. Socioeconomic development patterns reshape ecological baselines and influence EBR stability. EDA is objectively quantified through community-specific simulations, identifying vulnerable sub-watersheds requiring priority intervention. ERP relies significantly on the functional integrity of essential land types, where local degradation creates systemic recovery risks. A classification scheme with eight resilience types (T1–T8) is developed, supporting a dual-zone management strategy: adaptive enhancement and key control zones. The resilience assessment framework enables spatially explicit, dynamically responsive assessment of disaster-related ecological resilience at the community scale. It provides a replicable approach for identifying vulnerability hotspots and tailoring resilience-based risk management strategies. This research advances the integration of ecological resilience theory, disaster simulation, and actionable spatial planning for adaptive governance in hazard-prone community landscapes.

title: Bird-mediated cultural ecosystem services and disservices depend on urban residents’ perceptions of birds
abstract: Urbanization influences how people interact with nature, modifying perceptions of nature’s benefits (ecosystem services) or harms (ecosystem disservices or ED). In urban areas, wildlife-mediated ecosystem services remain understudied despite their importance for human well-being, particularly cultural ecosystem services (CES). The provision of species-mediated CES and ED also depends on the composition of wildlife communities, which can vary within cities. Urban areas can be developed in a gradient that goes from a scattered development (low-density housing with dispersed green spaces such as gardens) to a clumped development (high-density housing with large green spaces such as parks). Previous studies suggest that species composition, including CES and ED providers, may shift along this gradient. Yet, it remains unclear whether variation in these services and disservices is driven by differences in human perception (i.e., perception hypothesis) or by changes in ecological provision (i.e., species assembly hypothesis). We investigated both hypotheses using a multidisciplinary approach combining 637 in-person surveys and bird censuses across three Mediterranean cities. Our study identified four key CES (identity, educational, inspirational and bequest), disservices, and their main service-providing species. CES and ED varied across the gradient (i.e. higher bequest in clumped development while higher disservices in scattered development), mainly due to differences in residents’ perceptions rather than changes in the underlying ecological provision. Perceptions were also shaped by socio-demographic factors. This information can help create conservation plans to enhance the perception of benefits and promoting CES-providing species, while minimizing the harms associated with urban birds.

title: The restorative power of blue spaces: A 19-country study
abstract: Living in urbanised areas can deplete cognitive and emotional resources. To help restore them, many people seek out natural locations. Blue spaces (e.g. rivers, lakes, coasts) are among people’s favourite restorative settings, but we know little about the importance of type or quality for psychological restoration, or the role of nature connectedness. Using survey data from 19 countries (n = 17,131), we explored the extent to which participants perceived a recent blue space visit had helped them “rest and recover [their] abilities to focus” and feel “part of nature”. Seventeen blue space types were investigated, spanning marine, lentic (‘standing’) inland, and lotic (‘flowing’) inland waters in both more natural and more built settings, respectively. Accounting for country differences, linear mixed models found all blue space settings were recalled as restorative, with sandy beaches and rural rivers/canals the most, and marshlands the least. Recalled nature connectedness was also high overall, although more natural blue spaces consistently scored higher than built ones. Perceived safety was the quality indicator most associated with both outcomes. Actively engaging with the water (e.g. swimming, paddling) was associated with greater restoration than remaining on-land, and both outcomes showed diminishing marginal returns over time, peaking around 3 h. Path analysis focusing on walking (the most common visit activity) suggested a reciprocal relationship between perceived restoration and nature connectedness. Results provide multi-country evidence that spending recreational time at safe blue spaces can benefit diverse populations by helping them to restore depleted cognitive/emotional resources and connect with the natural world.

High-resolution pavement material data can improve estimates of water supply from precipitation to street trees
abstract: Impervious surfaces in urban landscapes strongly influence how precipitation supplies water to trees. Most data on imperviousness are satellite-derived, restricting our ability to analyze impacts of imperviousness at the scale of single tree catchments: the area covering tree roots. To address this challenge, we compiled a high-resolution dataset for Berlin, Germany, that specifies pavement materials and complemented it with hydrologic properties from the literature. Our approach aims to assess the accuracy of satellite-derived imperviousness in 71,311 tree catchments and analyze estimated infiltration reduction due to the presence of pavement at the local, fine scale. We found substantial disagreement with satellite-derived imperviousness for ≈ 99 % of tree catchments, and that satellite-derived data on average underestimate imperviousness by 13.1 %. High-resolution imperviousness correlated with reduced infiltration, yet catchments with similar imperviousness exhibited high variability and even bimodal distributions. These patterns can be explained by the dominant pavement material, highlighting the importance of high-resolution imperviousness data that capture pavement materials when assessing urban stormwater dynamics. In Berlin, the estimated mean annual infiltration reduction was 45.9 %. Applying the data in an illustrative case study suggested Tilia trees with possible annual water supply below transpiration demand during the growing season. These results indicate that street trees in paved environments might experience modified climatic and hydraulic regimes decoupled from those dictated by regional climates. Our findings can help refine predictions of tree drought stress and stimulate field studies along imperviousness gradients. The outcomes can inform practice, e.g., tree water management, and climate adaptation strategies in urban planning, such as pavement removal or retrofitting tree planting sites.

title: Beyond the buffer: an activity-based approach to heat exposure assessment
abstract: Due to the global climate crisis, heatwaves will become more frequent and severe in the future, leading to direct and indirect negative health effects. Heat affects places differently, as a result of built environment characteristics, which lead to different outdoor microclimates. This makes it important to assess in what locations people are most exposed to heat. Existing approaches assess this exposure mostly based on residence-based buffers or administrative units, which comes with contextual uncertainties, since it is not known to what extent hot or cool locations are actually traversed by residents. This is relevant because microclimates are highly local, which may make area-based assessments inaccurate. This paper therefore proposes and develops a different method, focusing on routes from residences to daily destinations. Results show that the microclimate in buffers or neighbourhoods is only moderately related to this activity-based heat exposure metric. The presence of green infrastructure within a buffer is related to the relative difference between the two exposure metrics: if an area is greener, activity-based exposure is relatively underestimated, and vice versa. A possible reason for this is that green space is often not traversed by routes to daily amenities. The results of this paper can be used to more carefully prioritize interventions that improve protection from hot microclimates, specifically by providing cooling in locations traversed by a large number of people.

Pollinator habitat enhancement through ornamental plants, floral traits and urban green area features for planning biodiversity-friendly cities
abstract: Ornamental plants are chosen for aesthetics or suitability to urban conditions, while their contribution to habitat enhancement is usually not a priority. However, studies have shown that ornamentals could have potential for pollinators. It is a priority to rank ornamental plants, and to understand which floral traits or environmental conditions influence visitation by pollinators, for habitat enhancement and landscape planning. Here, we surveyed ornamental plant–pollinator interactions across seven Italian cities, in May, to quantify relative plant attractiveness in field conditions, elucidate flower trait-pollinator relationships, and assess habitat descriptors or green area type influences. By focusing on plant-pollinator interactions, 43 ornamental plants were ranked for the contribution to both pollinator abundance and species richness, or to specific groups or few insects. Single floral traits positively or negatively associated with specific insect groups: these diverse responses clarify that trait diversity is essential to support heterogeneous urban pollinators. Furthermore, more abundant and species-rich pollinators were found on plants in heterogeneous area conditions, and distinctions emerged across parks, historic villas and botanic gardens. Therefore, apart from intrinsic plant features, the design and management of green areas should focus on adequate ornamental plants with diverse floral traits and in heterogeneous habitat contexts, to develop urban green infrastructures for pollinators. Landscape planning and management of green areas could integrate biodiversity-based strategies with priority ornamental plants for pollinator interactions, or use flower traits when lists are not available, to trigger urban ecosystem functionality and enhance habitat quality.
